Recent evidence complicates the assumption that multi-agent decomposition is beneficial by default: compute-normalized comparisons report that single agents match or exceed multi-agent systems at equal reasoning budgets, and failure analyses attribute a large share of multi-agent breakdowns to specification and inter-agent verification rather than to component capability. This paper takes that evidence as its starting point and asks a narrower question: which architectural properties, as opposed to which agent topology, determine whether an enterprise agentic workflow is governable, recoverable, and auditable. Recent evidence complicates the assumption that multi-agent decomposition is beneficial by default: compute-normalized comparisons report that single agents match or exceed multi-agent systems at equal reasoning budgets, and failure analyses attribute a large share of multi-agent breakdowns to specification and inter-agent verification rather than to component capability. This paper takes that evidence as its starting point and asks a narrower question: which architectural properties, as opposed to which agent topology, determine whether an enterprise agentic workflow is governable, recoverable, and auditable. We formalize an enterprise agentic workflow as a policy-constrained stateful system over agents, tools, workflow state, authorization policies, and human decision points, and establish four elementary results. First, policy soundness is a property of complete mediation of external actions and is independent of agent policy quality, which implies that it survives prompt injection and model failure whereas prompt-level guardrails do not. Second, recoverability and auditability require a durable external projection of every state component on which a consequential decision depends; context-resident state admits observationally indistinguishable histories with divergent correct continuations. Third, under an explicit independence idealization, sequential decomposition into n bounded agents without inter-stage verification bounds end-to-end success by p n , so the value of decomposition is conditioned on handoff verification rather than on specialization, which is consistent with reported empirical failure taxonomies. Fourth, attributability follows from complete mediation together with a total authorization relation over consequential actions and append-only logging. We map these results onto a five-layer reference architecture, a six-stage adoption protocol with explicit exit evidence, and a multi-level evaluation framework. We then specify a comparative evaluation protocol and an accompanying task schema that make the architecture falsifiable, including the configurations, metrics, and reporting requirements needed to test whether coordination earns its cost. The analytic results are proved; the architectural and adoption claims are stated as testable propositions and are not empirically validated here. We state explicitly which claims require experiment and what evidence would refute them.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7562798\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7515259\", \"title\": [\"Verification Independence for Agentic AI: Designing Review Beyond Self-Correction and Multi-Agent Agreement\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p><div>\\n As agentic artificial intelligence systems increasingly produce, evaluate, and act on their own outputs, review architectures face a structural problem: adding a second judgment does not necessarily create an independent basis for judgment. This paper proposes verification independence as a task-level design property for agentic AI. Verification independence asks whether the review process is sufficiently separated from the production process to surface errors that the producer is systematically unlikely to detect. The framework distinguishes four dimensions of independence: framing, evidence, mechanism, and authority. It also formalizes a four-function review architecture consisting of a producer, challenger, evidence checker, and acceptance owner.\\n</div>\\n<div>\\n <br>\\n</div>\\n<div>\\n The framework is positioned relative to research on LLM self-correction, chain-of-verification, multi-agent debate, LLM-as-a-judge, correlated model errors, and emerging agentic verification systems. Existing work shows both the value and limits of additional model-based review: structured verification can improve outputs, while multi-agent agreement, self-critique, and LLM judging remain vulnerable to shared assumptions, correlated errors, evaluator bias, and noisy rubric verification. The contribution here is integrative rather than a claim that any individual verification technique is new. It treats independence as a property of the relationship between production and review, not as a synonym for reviewer count or model diversity.\\n</div>\\n<div>\\n <br>\\n</div>\\n<div>\\n The central claim is that a reviewer can provide another judgment without providing another independent basis for judgment. For consequential agentic workflows, reliable verification therefore requires deliberate separation of review roles and, where feasible, external evidence, deterministic tests, independent tools, or distinct authority boundaries. The paper further introduces a qualitative independence checklist, risk-adjusted verification depth, and safeguards against erosion of independence in long-horizon workflows.\\n</div></jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7515259\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.54499/prt/bd/155071/2024\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.54499/prt/bd/155071/2024\"}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6774579\", \"title\": [\"Trustworthy Transaction Arena (TTA): A Governance Architecture for Multi-Actor Agentic AI Systems with Probabilistic Workflow Verification\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Existing multi-agent frameworks evaluate correctness only at the team outcome level: if the agent team achieves its goal, the transaction is deemed successful. This is insufficient for business and social activities, which consist of multiple interrelated tasks — involving asynchronous, time-constrained, and probabilistic behaviors — pursued toward broader goals. Without a framework that conveys objectives and authority to every actor throughout the activity, the means by which goals are achieved cannot be verified. This paper proposes the Trustworthy Transaction Arena (TTA), treating these activities as governed workflows in which every actor operates under delegated authority from a human principal, subject to continuous enforcement at every step. Its principal features — absent from all existing approaches — are: (i) a Unified Governance Layer combining static role-based and dynamic workflow-state access control in a single enforcement layer through which every actor action must pass; (ii) Non-Escalation of Delegated Authority (NEDA) — no agent can exceed the authority scope of its delegating principal — enforced transitively throughout the entire delegation chain; and (iii) a HERT probabilistic workflow engine handling asynchronous and stochastic behaviors, enabling critical path identification, bottleneck extraction, and detection of stochastic behaviors such as hallucination and capability leakage, with structural human supervision checkpoints. The architecture extends two production-validated prior works — the CBA access control model extended to cascaded AI agent delegation [Kitajima2002], and the HERT probabilistic formalism extended to stochastic workflow verification in AI environments [Kitajima1981-HERT] — and is demonstrated through an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest emergency response application.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6774579\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "3dd66f798e2d20b5ca5b800bfa4f926148e5aea75d629627c0e19411f60de015", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "unassigned_problem", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.7562798", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.7515259", "doi:10.54499/prt/bd/155071/2024", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.6774579"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7562798", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7515259", "https://doi.org/10.54499/prt/bd/155071/2024", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6774579"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
